bull_case: Rocket Lab is moving from dedicated small launch into an integrated stack of launch, spacecraft, components, deployable infrastructure and, if Iridium closes, spectrum plus recurring satellite services. Electron's cadence and 90+ launch backlog show adoption while Neutron could extend the model into medium lift.
bear_case: Electron is a strong niche product rather than a 10x cost revolution, Neutron is unflown, and Iridium is an acquisition of an existing network rather than a newly created market. Competitors with deeper balance sheets can respond, so the disruption claim depends on integration and execution rather than technology narrative alone.
thesis: Rocket Lab qualifies as a meaningful disruptive innovator, but the disruption is primarily value-chain integration and responsiveness rather than a proven 10x unit-cost break. Electron had 16 launches in 2026 through September 11, the launch backlog exceeds 90 missions, and the company is adding HASTE/GHOST, Neutron, spacecraft, GEO platforms, optical terminals and potentially Iridium's spectrum/network. This is a credible transition from component supplier and launcher toward an end-to-end space platform. The main constraint is that Neutron has not yet flown and Iridium has not closed.

evidence.claim: Rocket Lab completed its 16th Electron launch of 2026 and 95th overall by September 11, supporting a repeat-use, high-cadence dedicated launch model.
Q2 updates reported a launch backlog above 90 missions and more than $437M of new launch contracts across Electron, HASTE and Neutron.
Kepler booked a dedicated Neutron launch no earlier than 2028; Rocket Lab said the contract pushes Neutron's manifest toward full capacity through the end of the decade.

Rocket Lab introduced GHOST, a containerized deployable launch system intended to enable Electron/HASTE campaigns from geographically distributed sites, with first operational location planned in Alaska.
The Iridium transaction would add proprietary L-band spectrum, a global communications network, 500+ partners and recurring satellite services to Rocket Lab's launch and spacecraft stack.
Rocket Lab was awarded a $266M U.S. Space Force contract for 12 suborbital launches with up to six additional launches, expanding the responsive-defense launch value pool.

counterevidence: Electron's dedicated-launch proposition improves schedule control and responsiveness, but public evidence does not establish a 10x cost advantage versus alternatives.
Neutron's first flight was moved to Q4 2026 after a stage-1 tank qualification failure; launch-vehicle development remains a material technical-risk path.
Iridium's network and spectrum are acquired assets, so part of the platform expansion is capital allocation rather than organic disruption.
Government demand is important; H1 2026 government revenue exposure was 42%, so adoption is not purely commercial.
unknowns: Neutron delivered cost/kg, reuse turnaround and flight reliability after first launch.
Economics of GHOST deployments across multiple sites.
Incremental customer retention or pricing power created by combining Iridium services with Rocket Lab launch and spacecraft.
Share of future launch backlog that converts at attractive gross margin.
falsifiers: If Neutron cannot achieve repeat flight and customer launches after first flight, the medium-lift disruption thesis fails.
If launch backlog grows while launch gross economics deteriorate, adoption would not prove value creation.
If Iridium integration does not create cross-sell or constellation-replenishment economics, end-to-end platform optionality is overstated.

hard_veto_flags.rationale: Repeated Electron launches, multi-launch commercial bookings, a $2.36B backlog and contracted U.S. government missions show paid adoption rather than marketing-only demand.

Core innovation has real revenue and backlog, but Neutron development and the Iridium acquisition are capital intensive. Financial-survival analysis should determine whether this becomes structural dependence.

key_kpis.name: annual Electron/HASTE launches
key_kpis.threshold: cadence growth with high mission success

key_kpis.name: Neutron booked and completed missions
key_kpis.threshold: repeat commercial missions after first flight

subscores.rationale: Electron/HASTE plus GHOST materially change dedicated and responsive access by combining cadence, tailored orbit and deployability. This is above sustaining improvement but below 90 because a 10x cost/performance advantage is not publicly demonstrated.
16 launches by Sep. 11, 95 total flights, 90+ launch backlog and repeated constellation bookings indicate adoption well beyond pilot stage. Neutron remains unflown, preventing a 90 score.

Rocket Lab has entered multiple adjacent value pools—launch, spacecraft/components, responsive defense launch, GEO platforms/optical communications, and pending network/spectrum services. The portfolio is broad, but Rocket Lab does not yet define an industry-wide standard, so the 85 anchor is not fully met.

uncertainties.rationale: Public evidence supports responsiveness and integration more strongly than a quantified 10x cost curve.
Electron adoption is proven but Neutron, which is central to the next scale step, is pre-flight.
The Iridium transaction is pending and the economic interaction among launch, spacecraft and services is not yet observed.
